ontology-to-lpg#

From ontology-to-lpg/README.md

An agent skill for projecting an ontology built on the W3C stack (RDF, RDFS, OWL, SKOS, SHACL) into a Neo4j labelled property graph. The agent works in seven gated steps: design rules, inputs, check, reason and serialise, load, verify, and running it in a repository. The result is a graph that holds exactly the triples that passed every shape, and loads the same way every time. The Turtle release stays the master copy.

The skill is version 2.3 of the Ontology-to-LPG Conversion Playbook. Version 2.2 lived in the enterprise-people-graph repository; on 2026-10-23 the owner decided to move the guideline into this skill, and the repositories that kept a copy now point here. Version 2.3 adds what a projection of a multi-module enterprise ontology learned in October 2026, written in neutral terms with a library example. references/versions.md lists the changes.

This README is for people. Agents read SKILL.md and the files it points to.

Where it fits. The ontology skill's guide (references/playbook.md and references/ontology-build-playbook.html in that skill) is the method for building the ontology, and its Step 12 hands over to this skill. This playbook is the method for projecting the releases: the Turtle release stays the master copy, the checks prove the projection lost nothing, and references/multi-store.md covers another graph beside the projection and keeping the stores in step. The ontology guide's "The documents around this guide" lists what a project keeps beside these two methods. Both stay company-neutral.

How to use it#

  1. Install the skill where your agent finds skills, and ask the agent to project your ontology into Neo4j, or to check whether it is ready for a projection.
  2. The agent starts at the design rules and asks you to record the Rule 4 option and its reason in your projection policy. If the ontology is not released yet, it stops there and applies the rules before the first release.
  3. After a release, it fills a copy of templates/projection-config.json with you: the Rule 4 option and reason, your namespaces and prefixes, your released packages, your qualified-relation classes. It lists each rule gap in a released module as a release exception, with the release that will close it.
  4. Run the checks the agent runs: 
    uv run --no-project --with rdflib python3 scripts/check_projection_rules.py --config projection-config.json \
  --shapes <shapes.ttl> --releases <release folder> <module.ttl>
uv run --no-project --with rdflib --with pyshacl python3 scripts/validate_data.py --config projection-config.json \
  --shapes <shapes.ttl> <module.ttl>

    Each prints one line per failure and exits 1, or prints a pass line and exits 0.

  1. scripts/build.py writes the reasoner's input, the N-Triples files, the load script and the manifest; scripts/in_graph_shapes.py writes the shapes n10s can import without breaking; scripts/load_verify.py loads, reads back what n10s compiled, tests every compiled row, verifies and writes the report only when every check passed. Reason, load and verify run on a workstation with Java and Docker; references/running.md gives the jar checksums, the docker run line and what CI runs instead.

The ontology skill builds the ontology and hands over to this one at its Step 12. Each skill works without the other.

Common tasks#

Change a rule. Edit the reference file that holds it; SKILL.md only points. Keep each rule in one place, with its reason and a source in SOURCES.md.

A new n10s release. Run load_verify.py on the library templates with a shape for every term in the new version: the listShapes() comparison and the fail cases (references/pipeline.md, rules 13 and 14) show what changed. Then compare the new SHACLValidator.java with N10S_DATATYPES, INVERSE_UNREAD, the prediction queries and every cited line number in scripts/in_graph_shapes.py. Update them, references/pipeline.md, rules 13 and 14, the jar checksums in references/running.md, rule 2, and the versions in SOURCES.md.

A compiled row it cannot build a case for (such as sh:nodeKind sh:BlankNode, or a row on a sh:targetQuery shape) fails the run until --manual-cases gives one. copy_graph.py was run against a second local Neo4j and against Aura Free; triplestore.py against Apache Jena Fuseki 6.2.0. model_review.py ran on 2026-10-25 against a throwaway Neo4j 2025.06.2 holding small hand-made graphs: every query executed, the missing-constraint ERROR appeared and cleared once the constraint existed, and the reciprocal query returned only a real reciprocal pair (one edge between nodes that share labels was not reported). Its supernode rules found no hub there; they are tested on a fake that emulates its queries. It has not yet run on a projected ontology.

Design rules: what the ontology must do so the projection needs no guesses#

From references/design-rules.md

Serves the design step. Read it before an ontology that will be projected is modelled, or before its first release. A rule adopted after a release forces a new release of every module that breaks it. Examples use a library: works, people, copies, loans. Base https://id.example.org/library/, prefix lib:.

What the projection keeps#

KeptHow
Every individual, type, literal value and linkNodes, labels, properties, relationships
Facts about one link (a role, an order, a source, a validity period)Properties of a qualified-relation node (Rule 4a), or of a relationship (Rule 4b)
Class and property hierarchy, domains and rangesSchema nodes from n10s.onto.import; in SHORTEN mode :n4sch__Class, :n4sch__Relationship and :n4sch__Property, linked by n4sch__SCO, n4sch__DOMAIN and n4sch__RANGE
Cardinality and constraintsSHACL: every shape before the load, and inside the graph what the engine compiled, read back and tested row by row (pipeline.md, rules 13 and 14)
A full round trip back to RDFAn automated diff (pipeline.md, verify)

Not kept: OWL reasoning (open world, complex class expressions, property chains). Neo4j has no reasoner. The pipeline runs one first and loads its inferences as data. The axioms stay in the Turtle files, which stay the master copy.

Background. The research closest to these rules is S3PG (Rabbani, Lissandrini, Bonifati and Hose, Proceedings of the ACM on Management of Data 2(6), 2024, https://doi.org/10.1145/3698817), which drives the RDF-to-property-graph conversion from SHACL shapes and emits PG-Schema (Angles and others, Proceedings of the ACM on Management of Data 1(2), 2023, https://doi.org/10.1145/3589778). Like Rules 1 and 2 here, it lets the shapes decide whether a value becomes a property or a relationship, and how many values it may have. Neo4j's neo4j-modeling-skill is background for the same two rules from the graph side. This skill does not run S3PG; the rules stand on the n10s runs recorded in SOURCES.md.

Where this skill departs from neo4j-modeling-skill#

Neo4j's neo4j-modeling-skill (version 1.0.7, read 2026-10-24) is written for graphs designed in Cypher. A projection keeps what the ontology says, so three of its defaults do not apply here. scripts/model_review.py checks the rules the projection does keep (add-ons.md, "Reviewing the loaded graph").

  • A SKOS concept or code-list value stays a node. The modeling skill says, of low-cardinality state such as a status: "Never a (:Status) node." In a projection a concept carries an IRI, a definition, a place in a hierarchy (skos:broader), mappings and a source, which a label cannot hold. So rdf:type gives labels and every concept stays a node, as the mental model below shows. model_review.py counts a concept's relationships in both directions: one at ten times its label's median degree (and at least 50) is a WARNING supernode candidate, and one above 100,000 a WARNING supernode. Either is read against the ontology; neither turns the concept into a label.
  • A link may carry properties. The modeling skill's decision table answers "Does the connection have its own properties or multiple targets?" with "Intermediate node", and it promotes a relationship that "has >2 properties". Here Rule 4 decides: under 4a a link that carries facts already is a qualified-relation node; under 4b a reifier's literal properties sit on the relationship. A property count alone never promotes a link.
  • One local heuristic is added. model_review.py's reciprocal-type (INFO) flags one relationship type used from label A to B and from B to A. The modeling skill asks only that direction carry meaning ("Rel direction encodes semantic meaning"); it does not forbid this. In a projection the pattern usually means one ontology property stated both ways where a property and its inverse were meant, so the review points at it without calling it an anti-pattern.
  • The questions come from the ontology. Its first default, "list 5+ queries the model must answer before designing", is met by the ontology's competency questions, written as SPARQL and run against the release (the ontology skill). The projection answers the same questions in Cypher; it adds none of its own.

Mental model#

literal object            -> node property
IRI object                -> relationship
rdf:type                  -> label
qualified-relation node   -> node with its own IRI, linked to both ends (Rule 4a)
reifier (rdf:reifies)     -> properties on that relationship (Rule 4b)
everything else           -> stays in the Turtle files

The five rules#

Each rule can be checked by a script; scripts/check_projection_rules.py checks Rules 1, 2, 3, 4a and the Rule 5 names.

  1. Give every property you own exactly one kind, and every object or datatype property one concrete range. The kinds are owl:ObjectProperty, owl:DatatypeProperty and owl:AnnotationProperty. n10s itself decides from each value, not from the kind: an IRI value loads as a relationship and a literal as a node property, so an annotation property with IRI values (rdfs:seeAlso <...>) loads as relationships. The kind and range are what the checks, the multivalued list and the XSD to Cypher table read. A concrete range is one IRI: for a datatype property, a datatype in the XSD to Cypher table below (an unlisted XSD type, rdf:HTML or a custom rdfs:Datatype fails); for an object property, a class; never rdfs:Literal or rdfs:Resource, never a bare rdf:Property. An annotation property needs no range. A property counts as yours when its IRI is in one of your namespaces and it is used as a predicate, declared with a property kind, or given a domain, a range or a parent property. Prefer zoned xsd:dateTimeStamp for timestamps. Why: the checks, the multivalued list and the XSD to Cypher table read the kind and the range; with one of each, every value of the property is either an IRI (a relationship) or a literal of one type (a property of one Cypher type, table below). A vague range lets values of both sorts in, and the property then loads as relationships for some subjects and properties for others. 
    lib:barcode   a owl:DatatypeProperty ; rdfs:range xsd:string .   # literal values: a node property
lib:copyOf    a owl:ObjectProperty   ; rdfs:range lib:Work .     # IRI values: a relationship
lib:shelfNote a owl:AnnotationProperty .                         # literal values here: a node property
  1. State a cardinality for every property you own in SHACL: sh:maxCount 1 for a single value; sh:minCount with no sh:maxCount for a list (write sh:minCount 0 for an optional list, so the choice is stated). Annotation properties too. The cardinality counts only on a property shape that an applied shape uses: one with any target (sh:targetClass, sh:targetNode, sh:targetSubjectsOf, sh:targetObjectsOf, a SHACL-SPARQL sh:target), one that is itself a class, or one reached from those through sh:node, sh:and, sh:or or sh:xone. A loose shape with the same sh:path states nothing. The check covers the properties the data uses; a property declared but not yet used loads nothing, so it needs its cardinality only once data uses it (the ontology skill's shape rules still ask for it at release). Why: sh:maxCount 1 loads one value and anything else loads a sorted array; the loader's list of multi-valued properties is generated from the shapes, so an unstated cardinality is a guess. 
    lib:CopyShape a sh:NodeShape ; sh:targetClass lib:Copy ;
  sh:property [ sh:path lib:barcode ; sh:datatype xsd:string ; sh:minCount 1 ; sh:maxCount 1 ] ;
  sh:property [ sh:path lib:copyOf  ; sh:class lib:Work ; sh:minCount 1 ; sh:maxCount 1 ] .
lib:WorkShape a sh:NodeShape ; sh:targetClass lib:Work ;
  sh:property [ sh:path lib:altTitle ; sh:datatype rdf:langString ; sh:minCount 0 ] .   # a sorted array
  1. Give every individual a permanent IRI, put no blank node in the data, and register one fixed prefix per namespace. Never generate IRIs per run. Qualified-relation nodes and reifiers need IRIs most, because the IRI becomes the node's or relationship's uri in the graph. Register a prefix for every namespace a predicate or a class uses, your own and the standard ones, wherever the class appears: as a type, a declared class, a superclass, a domain or range, or a shape's target or sh:class. A datatype range counts too, so xsd: needs its prefix; and never two prefixes for one namespace. Why: in SHORTEN mode n10s names a term by its namespace's prefix, two underscores and the local name (lib__barcode), and invents a numbered ns prefix for a namespace it does not know; fixed prefixes make the names the same on every load.
  1. Choose one pattern for links that carry properties, record it, and use it everywhere. Rule 4 covers a link whose only job is to carry facts about one relationship. A link the business tracks as a thing in its own right is a domain class instead, outside Rule 4: it has its own identity or lifecycle, and other records refer to it. A lib:Loan is one: it has a loan number, and fines and renewals point at it. Why: mixing patterns makes the conversion code guess which one a link uses.

    4a, the default: qualified-relation nodes. The link becomes a node with its own IRI that points at both ends, the pattern of W3C ORG's org:Membership and PROV-O's qualified relations. It is plain RDF, so rdflib, pySHACL, Jena, RDF4J and n10s all read it, and it needs no flatten step.

    <https://id.example.org/library/authorship/W-0042-P-17> a lib:Authorship ;
    lib:authorshipAgent <https://id.example.org/library/person/P-17> ;
    lib:creatorRole lib:illustrator ;
    lib:position 2 ;
    lib:source "Catalogue record 0042, field 700" .
<https://id.example.org/library/work/W-0042> lib:hasAuthorship <https://id.example.org/library/authorship/W-0042-P-17> .

    In the graph this is a :lib__Authorship node with its properties, a relationship to the person, and one from the work.

    • Give each qualified-relation node exactly one value for each end, with sh:minCount 1 ; sh:maxCount 1 on each end's property in a shape that targets the qualified-relation class. The checker fails when that shape is missing, even while the data happens to hold one value.
    • An end may point at the node instead, by an inverse link (lib:hasAuthorship above, like prov:qualifiedAssociation or org:hasMembership). Count that link as the end, check that exactly one such link points at each node, and shape it from the node's side with sh:path [ sh:inversePath lib:hasAuthorship ] ; sh:minCount 1 ; sh:maxCount 1. n10s runs that inverse-path shape in the graph. Why: the arcs that define the node are not domain links, and the inverse form is the one PROV-O and ORG use.
    • Register every qualified-relation class with its ends in the projection's configuration (inputs.md, rule 3), and add each new one when a module defines it. Why: the rule check finds the nodes by their class.
    • If a consumer also wants a direct edge (work lib:createdBy person), assert that triple too, or derive it with a SPARQL CONSTRUCT before the load. Never hand-write it in Cypher.
    • Choose 4a while any tool in the pipeline lacks RDF 1.2 support.

    4b: RDF 1.2 reifiers. Use it only when every tool that reads and validates the data reads RDF 1.2 triple terms: Apache Jena 6.1.0 or later, or Eclipse RDF4J 6.0.0 or later. Jena 5.4.0 to 6.0.x was an experimental preview. rdflib and pySHACL do not read RDF 1.2, so a Python pipeline built on them uses 4a. n10s cannot load triple terms, so 4b needs the flatten step in pipeline.md. RDF 1.2 Concepts is a W3C Candidate Recommendation (Snapshot, 7 April 2026), not yet a Recommendation.

    <https://id.example.org/library/work/W-0042> lib:createdBy <https://id.example.org/library/person/P-17>
    ~ <https://id.example.org/library/authorship/W-0042-P-17> {| lib:position 2 |} .

    Rules for reifiers: one reifier gives one relationship, which carries the reifier's uri; two reifiers of one triple give two parallel relationships, never merged; an asserted triple with no reifier gives one plain relationship; a triple term that is not asserted gives a relationship with asserted: false, or is left out by a recorded exclusion (add-ons.md, D); a reifier's properties are literal-valued, and a link to another resource is stored as a string property such as approvedBy_uri, which the round trip restores.

  1. Name the graph explicitly only where the SHORTEN name is not good enough, through one annotation property (lpg:name), and check that no two terms share a name. n10s applies such mappings only in MAP mode, and the pipeline uses SHORTEN (pipeline.md, rule 9). So add the names as a generated, idempotent rename after the load, before verify, and reverse it before the round-trip export. Why: MAP mode breaks in-graph SHACL in n10s (neosemantics issue #237, open since 2021-11-09; its fix, PR #361, is open), and without the rename every name is already unique by construction.

Where the Rule 4 choice is recorded#

Record the Rule 4 option and its reason in the projection policy, and copy both into the configuration's rule4 and rule4_reason. The projection policy is the project's written decision to project the ontology into a property graph. Any recorded place that holds the option and its reason counts: for an ontology built with the ontology skill, policy 10 (target formats) in its templates/policies.md; otherwise a decision record the owner approved, or the project's own method. For the library example, the policy is the template configuration's rule4 and rule4_reason. Why: the policy is the decision, and the configuration is the copy the scripts read; every script of this skill (check_projection_rules.py, validate_data.py, build.py cypher, load_verify.py) stops with exit 2 under 4b, because each reads RDF 1.1 only.

OWL profile#

Keep reasoning within OWL 2 EL, and run ELK (pipeline.md, reason). EL has no inverse properties: store one direction per fact, and materialise the inverse before the load if consumers need it. Why: EL reasoning is fast and predictable on large hierarchies, and a property graph does no reasoning of its own.

XSD to Cypher types (fixed)#

XSDCypher
string, token, normalizedStringSTRING
booleanBOOLEAN
integer, long, int, nonNegativeIntegerINTEGER (64-bit, range-checked)
double, floatFLOAT
decimalFLOAT, or STRING with add-on C. Refuse a decimal whose value, printed as a double, is not its own lexical form (0.64 passes; 0.1000000000000000055 does not), or adopt add-on C
dateDATE
dateTimeStamp, or dateTime with a timezoneZONED DATETIME
dateTime without a timezoneLOCAL DATETIME (better: forbid it in SHACL)
durationDURATION
anyURISTRING
rdf:langString, rdf:dirLangString (RDF 1.2)STRING with the tag kept inside it (keepLangTag), or add-on B

Inputs: what the projection reads, and the gaps it may carry#

From references/inputs.md

Serves the inputs step. Read it before the first projection run, and whenever a module is released, added or given a new namespace. The configuration it describes is templates/projection-config.json. check_projection_rules.py, validate_data.py and build.py read it; in_graph_shapes.py reads only the shapes.

The configuration's keys:

KeyWhat it holds
rule4, rule4_reasonThe Rule 4 option (4a or 4b) and why, copied from the projection policy (design-rules.md, "Where the Rule 4 choice is recorded").
own_namespacesEvery namespace you own whose terms appear as predicates or classes (rule 3). A namespace that holds only individuals may be left out.
prefixesOne prefix per namespace, in the order the loader adds them (rules 3 and 4).
qualified_relationsEach qualified-relation class with its ends and inverse_ends (rule 3).
packagesEach released module's pinned version (rule 1).
release_exceptionsEach listed rule gap and its fix (rule 5).
versionsThe tool versions the run used (running.md, rule 2).
lpg_name_propertyOptional: the annotation property that carries Rule 5 names.

Data files and shape files are not in the configuration: pass them to each script on its command line (--shapes for shapes), in the same order every time, because the shapes fingerprint depends on the order.

Rules#

  1. Project the released packages, each at its newest version, not the working source files. Pin each module's version by hand in the configuration (packages), and check the pins against the release folder: the check fails when a module has a newer release than its pin, when a module has a release and no pin, and when a pin names a version with no release folder (check_projection_rules.py --releases <folder>). The release folder holds one folder per module, and in it one folder per release named by its version: <folder>/<module>/<X.Y.Z>/. Only names of the form X.Y.Z count as releases, so a candidate folder such as 1.2.0-rc.1 is ignored. For the library example, build the folder from the templates: mkdir -p releases/lending/1.1.0 && cp templates/library-module.ttl releases/lending/1.1.0/lending.ttl && cp templates/library-shapes.ttl releases/lending/1.1.0/shapes.ttl, then run the checker with --releases releases on releases/lending/1.1.0/lending.ttl. Each release folder holds the package the ontology's release step built: the module's Turtle (<module>.ttl), its shapes (shapes.ttl) and its manifest, with a DCAT record, a changelog and other formats beside them. The projection reads the module Turtle as data and shapes.ttl as shapes. Why: consumers get what was released, so the projection must test the releases; a pin by hand makes a new release a visible change, and the folder check stops the pin going stale. Where one module was released against an older version of another, the projection still takes each module's newest release; each package's own release checks keep testing the versions it pinned.
  1. Run each package's own shapes, plus every shape that checks the whole graph. Pass every package's shapes.ttl and every whole-graph shape file to each script with --shapes; the manifest fingerprints each one (running.md, rule 3). Why: a package's shapes are part of its release, and a cross-module shape catches a break that no single package's shapes can see.
  1. Apply Rules 1 and 2 to the predicates of every namespace you own whose terms are predicates or classes, and give each its fixed prefix. List in own_namespaces every namespace you own whose terms the data uses as predicates or classes (a namespace that holds only individuals, such as https://id.example.org/library/work/, may be left out: no rule checks an individual's namespace), and give it the prefix its package uses where it has one (prefixes). Register each qualified-relation class with its ends (qualified_relations, design-rules.md, rule 4). Why: a rule checked on one module lets every later module break it, and a namespace missing from the list is never checked.
  1. Register the standard namespaces too. Every namespace that a predicate or a class in the data uses (RDF, RDFS, OWL, SKOS, DCMI terms, ORG, PROV-O, DCAT, XSD and any other) needs one prefix in prefixes. Why: the loader adds exactly these prefixes, in this order, so n10s never invents one.
  1. List each rule gap in a released module as a release exception, with its fix, and fail on an unlisted gap or on a listed gap that no longer occurs. A gap in a released module (a property with no range, a property with no cardinality shape) can close only in that module's next release, because released packages never change. Only a Rule 1, Rule 2 or Rule 5 failure can be listed. Key each exception by the checker's exact message (a term may be written as a CURIE, as the checker prints it, or as a full IRI, bare or in angle brackets), and say in its fix which release closes it and what that release adds: 
    "release_exceptions": {
  "Rule 1: lib:shelfmark has no single concrete range":
    "lending 1.0.0 declares no rdfs:range; the next lending release adds rdfs:range xsd:string"
}

    Why: the list lets the projection run without hiding the gap; failing on a stale entry means the list always describes the releases, so it shrinks as releases close the gaps. A blank node, a missing prefix, a broken qualified relation, a refused value or a stale pin is a data error, not a release gap: the checker fails on it even when it is listed.

  1. When a release closes a gap, remove its exception in the same change that moves the pin. Why: the check fails until both are done, which is the point.

The pipeline: check, reason, serialise, load, verify#

From references/pipeline.md

Serves the pipeline steps. Read it before writing or changing the projection's code. The five steps work from ten triples to hundreds of millions; only the loader changes with scale (running.md, rule 6). The tool versions named here are the ones tested: Neo4j 2025.06.2 (Community edition), n10s (neosemantics) 2025.06.1 with APOC, ROBOT 1.9.10. Every script named here is in this skill's scripts/; run each with uv run --no-project --with rdflib python3 <script> (add --with pyshacl for validate_data.py, --with neo4j for load_verify.py). load_verify.py runs the load and verify sections below (SKILL.md steps 5 and 6) against the container end to end and writes the report; the rules below say what it does, so a project can also write its own.

 module.ttl ──┐
 shapes.ttl ──┤  check  ─▶  reason  ─▶  serialise  ─▶  load  ─▶  verify      (SKILL.md steps 3 to 6)
 config ──────┘  (rules,    (ELK,       (sorted N-Triples;  (n10s,    (SHACL in the graph,
                  SHACL)     once)       4b: flatten)        SHORTEN)  round trip, determinism)
PurposeTool
Parse RDF, run SPARQLRule 4a: rdflib, Jena or RDF4J. Rule 4b: Jena 6.1.0+ or RDF4J 6.0.0+
ReasonROBOT (robot reason --reasoner ELK)
ValidatepySHACL (Rule 4a only; it is built on rdflib) or Jena SHACL
Loadn10s
Diffrdflib compare, or Jena rdfcompare

The checks of these rules, numbered V1 to V12 in the order they run, are mapped in multi-store.md, "The validation path, V1 to V14, and GRAPH TYPE, G1 to G4".

Check (SKILL.md step 3)#

  1. Check the design rules over the ontology, then validate the data with every shape, and stop the build on any failure. Run check_projection_rules.py --config <config> --shapes <every shape file> --releases <folder> <every released data file>, then validate_data.py --config <config> --shapes <every shape file> <every released data file>, which runs pySHACL with SHACL-AF on (advanced=True, so SPARQL targets and constraints run) and the refusals of rule 3. Under Rule 4b every script of this skill stops with exit 2 (check_projection_rules.py, validate_data.py, build.py cypher and load_verify.py; rdflib cannot read triple terms): run the same checks in Jena SHACL or RDF4J, or stop and ask the owner which tool to use. Why: this is the full check; the graph later runs only a subset of the shapes (rule 13), so a constraint skipped here is never checked.
  1. After serialising, validate again over both output files together: validate_data.py --config <config> --shapes <every shape file> loadable.nt inferred.nt. Why: an inference can break a shape, and the graph holds both files.
  1. Refuse any value that cannot survive the round trip. Both scripts of rule 1 refuse, and no release exception waives either:
    • a plain or xsd:string literal that matches @[A-Za-z]{1,8}(-[A-Za-z0-9]{1,8})*$ (it ends like a language tag, such as "Spine@en"). n10s stores a tagged literal as "text@en", so it would read such a string back as tagged text;
    • an xsd:decimal whose nearest double, printed in its shortest form and read back as a decimal, does not equal its value. "1" (back as 1.0), "0.64" and "12.5" survive; "0.1000000000000000055" (back as 0.1) does not. Change the value, or adopt add-on C.

    Why: the round-trip comparison (rule 16) treats these as equal or as tagged, so it would hide a real change.

Reason (SKILL.md step 4)#

  1. Reason once, upstream, with ELK through ROBOT, over the merged released data: 
    uv run --no-project --with rdflib python3 build.py merge --output merged.ttl <every released data file>
java -jar robot.jar reason --reasoner ELK --input merged.ttl \
  --axiom-generators "SubClass ClassAssertion" --include-indirect true --output reasoned.ttl

    Check robot.jar against its SHA-256 first (running.md, rule 2).

    merged.ttl holds every released data file (each package's module Turtle) and nothing else: no shapes, no inferred triples, no configuration. ELK is ROBOT's default reasoner. By default reason asserts only inferred subclass axioms, so name ClassAssertion to get inferred types too, and it asserts only direct ones, so add --include-indirect true: without it, an individual asserted as a lib:Book gets only its direct type, which is already asserted, and nothing is inferred. ROBOT fails the step on an incoherent ontology (an inconsistency or an unsatisfiable class). With the flag, inferred.nt holds every entailed type and superclass link, indirect ones included, except OWL and RDFS built-ins: a node then carries a label for each of its classes, so MATCH (:lib__Work) finds books. That is intended, and it does what add-on A asks for. To load only the asserted types, leave the flag out and accept that only axioms which change an individual's most specific type produce inferences. Why: a property graph does no OWL reasoning, so inferences must arrive as data.

Serialise (SKILL.md step 4)#

  1. Write loadable.nt and inferred.nt as sorted, de-duplicated N-Triples, and record the input fingerprint. uv run --no-project --with rdflib python3 build.py loadable --output loadable.nt <every released data file>. Sorted means one triple per line, lines ordered by their UTF-8 bytes, duplicates removed: the order LC_ALL=C sort -u gives. The input fingerprint is the SHA-256 of the bytes of loadable.nt followed directly by the bytes of inferred.nt (one hash over the concatenation, not a hash of the two hashes); build.py manifest computes it. In this order, after rule 6: first check both files with uv run --no-project --with rdflib python3 build.py check-serialised --loadable loadable.nt --inferred inferred.nt: it fails unless each line is exactly one triple and nothing else (no comment, trailing or whole-line), the lines are in byte order without duplicates, and inferred.nt holds only kept inferences that loadable.nt does not already assert. Then validate both files together (rule 2). Only then write the manifest, without --verify on the first run: build.py manifest --config <config> --shapes <shapes>... --loadable loadable.nt --inferred inferred.nt --output projection-manifest.json <data>..., so it never fingerprints files those checks have not accepted (V4, then V5, in multi-store.md). It records each file's path relative to the manifest's own folder. Why: a fixed byte order makes the files diffable and their hash repeatable, and keeping inferences apart keeps them distinguishable from assertions.
  1. Build inferred.nt from the reasoner's input and output, compared as triples: uv run --no-project --with rdflib python3 build.py inferred --input merged.ttl --reasoned reasoned.ttl --output inferred.nt. It keeps the triples of reasoned.ttl that are not in merged.ttl, then only rdf:type and rdfs:subClassOf triples whose subject and object are both IRIs, then drops those whose object is in the OWL or RDFS namespace. If you build it with other tools, put both files through the same serialiser before comparing lines, or compare triples: two serialisers write the same triple differently. build.py check-serialised (rule 5) checks the result. Why: ROBOT writes through the OWL API, which declares every individual owl:NamedIndividual and adds owl:Class, owl:Thing, owl:AnnotationProperty and rdfs:Datatype declarations; they are new in the output but are not inferences about the domain. OWL axioms use blank nodes whose labels change from run to run, so a triple with a blank node never counts. On a SKOS-first ontology with few class axioms the file can rightly be empty; on the library template it holds one triple (W-0043 rdf:type lib:Work).
  1. Rule 4b only: flatten each reifier into a plain EdgeRecord node with SPARQL 1.2 (Jena 6.1.0+ or RDF4J 6.0.0+), then union, sort and de-duplicate. n10s cannot load triple terms, and RDF 1.1 N-Triples cannot write them. Check first that triple terms appear only as objects of rdf:reifies, so keep.rq drops nothing else. 
    # keep.rq: every triple whose object is not a triple term
CONSTRUCT { ?s ?p ?o } WHERE { ?s ?p ?o FILTER(!isTRIPLE(?o)) }
    # edges.rq: one EdgeRecord per reifier
PREFIX rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#>
PREFIX lpg: <https://id.example.org/lpg-mapping#>
CONSTRUCT { ?r a lpg:EdgeRecord ; lpg:edgeSource ?s ; lpg:edgePredicate ?p ; lpg:edgeTarget ?o ; lpg:asserted ?asserted . }
WHERE {
  ?r rdf:reifies ?tt .
  BIND(SUBJECT(?tt) AS ?s) BIND(PREDICATE(?tt) AS ?p) BIND(OBJECT(?tt) AS ?o)
  BIND(EXISTS { ?s ?p ?o } AS ?asserted)
}

    The 4b path has not been run end to end; the tested runs used 4a.

Load (SKILL.md step 5)#

Start the container first, as running.md, rule 5 says.

  1. Generate every Cypher statement from the ontology and the configuration, and give the database its four files. build.py cypher --config <config> --shapes <every shape file> --output load.cypher <every released data file> writes the load script to load.cypher (no script prints Cypher to the terminal). It reads four files from the import folder mounted at /import: merged.ttl (rule 4), shapes-in-graph.ttl (rule 13), loadable.nt and inferred.nt (rules 5 and 6). load_verify.py copies them there and runs the script one statement at a time, checking each result (rule 11). By hand, copy the four files into the import folder and run the script inside the container: . "<run folder>/run.env"; docker exec -i -e NEO4J_PASSWORD="$PASSWORD" "$CONTAINER" cypher-shell -u neo4j < load.cypher (the password goes in the environment, not on the command line) (running.md, rule 5). Use MERGE and SET with explicit ordering in anything you add. Why: hand-written Cypher drifts from the ontology, and n10s defaults are not deterministic (multivalued properties default to overwrite, and unknown namespaces get invented prefixes).
  1. Configure n10s with SHORTEN, not MAP, and add the configuration's prefixes in its order: 
    CREATE CONSTRAINT n10s_unique_uri IF NOT EXISTS FOR (r:Resource) REQUIRE r.uri IS UNIQUE;
CALL n10s.graphconfig.init({
  handleVocabUris: 'SHORTEN', handleRDFTypes: 'LABELS_AND_NODES',
  handleMultival: 'ARRAY', multivalPropList: [/* generated, rule 10 */],
  keepLangTag: true, keepCustomDataTypes: true });
CALL n10s.nsprefixes.add('lib', 'https://id.example.org/library/');   // one per prefix, in order

    Why: in MAP mode n10s 2025.06.1 would not import shapes ("The graph is not namespace aware"), and MAP gives every term without a mapping the IGNORE treatment, which drops its namespace and breaks the round trip. SHORTEN keeps both; in it n10s ignores n10s.mapping.add, so the Rule 5 names come from a rename (design-rules.md, rule 5).

  1. Generate the multivalued list by one rule, and sort arrays only on :Resource nodes. A predicate is literal-valued when any of its objects in the data is a literal. It goes in multivalPropList unless a property shape that an applied shape uses (any target kind, as design-rules.md, rule 2 defines it) gives its path sh:maxCount 1; it goes in anyway when one subject holds more than one literal value for it. So a standard predicate with no shape of its own (rdfs:label, skos:prefLabel, dcterms:title, owl:versionInfo) loads as an array, even with one value; give it a shape with sh:maxCount 1 if consumers need a single value. After the load, sort each listed key, by its SHORTEN name, on resource nodes only: 
    MATCH (n:Resource) WHERE n.`lib__altTitle` IS NOT NULL SET n.`lib__altTitle` = apoc.coll.sort(n.`lib__altTitle`);

    Never sort every list property on every node: n10s keeps its own configuration in nodes without the Resource label (_GraphConfig, _NsPrefDef, _n10sValidatorConfig), and sorting the byte arrays of _n10sValidatorConfig corrupts it, after which n10s.validation.shacl.listShapes() fails with StreamCorruptedException. Why: an array's order otherwise follows the load order, and the rule decides every predicate the same way on every load.

  1. Load in a fixed order and check each import:
    1. n10s.onto.import.fetch('file:///import/merged.ttl', 'Turtle'): the merged released data of rule 4, from which n10s builds its schema nodes (n4sch__Class and the rest);
    2. n10s.validation.shacl.import.fetch('file:///import/shapes-in-graph.ttl', 'Turtle'): the import-safe shapes of rule 13;
    3. n10s.rdf.import.fetch of loadable.nt, then of inferred.nt ('N-Triples').

    The two rdf.import calls and onto.import succeed when they return terminationStatus OK. The shapes import returns no terminationStatus: it returns one row per constraint it compiled, and it succeeds when that row count is above zero and equals the count of CALL n10s.validation.shacl.listShapes(). Record both counts in the report (shapes_import_rows, in_graph_shape_constraints). The two counts only show that the import finished; rule 13 compares the listed rows with the shapes file, row by row. The paths assume the import folder is mounted at /import (running.md, rule 5). n10s keeps no graph names, so asserted and inferred triples merge in the graph; the two files keep them apart (add-on F if the graph itself must tell them apart). Why: a fixed order and a checked result make the load repeatable and stop a partial import from passing.

    Keep n10s's names, or rename them once every check has passed. n10s writes prefix__local. When a run names another separator (separator in the run configuration, --separator on load_verify.py), the SHACL import, the fail cases, the mutant and the round trip all run on n10s's names, and only then is every label, relationship type and property key renamed with APOC (apoc.refactor.rename.label, .type, .nodeProperty, .typeProperty); a dump taken before the rename, with the expected renames applied, must equal the dump after (rename_lossless), and the determinism hashes are of the renamed graph. The in-graph SHACL cannot run after the rename (n10s needs its own names), which is why the order is fixed.

  1. Rule 4b only: after the load, turn each EdgeRecord into a relationship with properties, generated once per reified predicate with the predicate's SHORTEN name, then delete plain edges that duplicate a reified one: 
    MATCH (r:lpg__EdgeRecord)-[:lpg__edgeSource]->(s), (r)-[:lpg__edgeTarget]->(t),
      (r)-[:lpg__edgePredicate]->(p {uri: 'https://id.example.org/library/createdBy'})
WITH r, s, t ORDER BY r.uri
CALL apoc.merge.relationship(s, 'lib__createdBy', {uri: r.uri}, apoc.map.removeKeys(properties(r), ['uri']), t, {}) YIELD rel
DETACH DELETE r;
MATCH (s)-[plain]->(t), (s)-[reified]->(t)
WHERE type(plain) = type(reified) AND plain.uri IS NULL AND reified.uri IS NOT NULL
DELETE plain;

Shapes in the graph (SKILL.md step 5)#

  1. Withhold from the engine only what breaks it, then read back what it compiled: the readback is the gate. load_verify.py writes shapes-in-graph.ttl with in_graph_shapes.subset and imports it. The subset leaves out only the terms that make n10s 2025.06.1 throw on import or judge valid data wrong, each listed in the report's left_out_before_import with its reason:
    • sh:datatype outside n10s's list (xsd:boolean, xsd:string, xsd:integer, xsd:float, xsd:decimal, xsd:date, xsd:dateTime, xsd:anyURI, geo:wktLiteral; SHACLValidator.java at tag 2025.06.1, lines 1191 to 1209): n10s throws for any other, rdf:langString and xsd:dateTimeStamp among them;
    • sh:pattern (with sh:flags): n10s tests each value with Cypher =~, which matches the whole string, while SHACL searches it (SHACL §4.4.3, through SPARQL REGEX). An unanchored "\S" fails every value longer than one character in the graph and passes in pySHACL. Patterns are checked before the load only;
    • an sh:in list that holds a literal, and a literal sh:hasValue: n10s compares them as strings, so a loaded true did not match sh:in (true). IRI lists and IRI values stay;
    • a value term (sh:class, sh:in, sh:datatype, sh:nodeKind, sh:hasValue, sh:disjoint, ranges, lengths, sh:pattern) on an inverse path: n10s reads the inverse flag only for cardinality (line 580), so it checks the term against the outgoing relationships. In a load on 2026-10-23, sh:class on [ sh:inversePath p ] caught an outgoing p to an unclassed node and missed an incoming one. Counts on an inverse path stay: they ran the right way;
    • a shape with sh:deactivated true: SHACL skips it, and n10s does not read the flag;
    • an sh:message that holds a single quote: n10s writes each message into its check's Cypher as '%s' as customMsg, without escaping it (SHACLValidator.java at tag 2025.06.1, line 1232), so n10s.validation.shacl.validate() fails with a Cypher SyntaxException. In a load on 2026-10-26 it failed on sh:message "A customer system's definition cites its source.", and the same load passed with that message left out. A message on a shape n10s never compiles (one with sh:targetObjectsOf, say) does no harm, which is why an earlier message with a quote passed. The ontology skill's references/shacl.md, rule 19, keeps the quote out at the source.

    Everything else goes to the engine as written. What n10s does not read, it ignores; that is why the gate reads the engine, not the file. After the import, load_verify.py calls n10s.validation.shacl.listShapes() (https://neo4j.com/labs/neosemantics/4.3/validation/: it lists the loaded constraints, the same rows the import returns; in 2025.06.1 the columns are target, propertyOrRelationshipPath, param and value) and compares each row with the constraints the file states, by target, path, param and value. What the comparison found in the engine:

    • a property constraint is listed as (class, path, "sh:<term>", value), an inverse path without a marker, sh:nodeKind as "sh:NodeKind" with the full IRI, sh:class as the class's SHORTEN name, sh:in as a list of IRIs;
    • sh:disjoint is listed as "sh:hasValue" with the other property's IRI as a one-member list; it runs as a disjoint check (rule 14 tests it) and is the one documented exception to "param names the term";
    • sh:closed true is listed as (class, null, "sh:ignoredProperties", [the ignored properties]), and a node-level sh:class as (class, null, "sh:class", class).

    Every constraint of the file with no matching row is printed (NOT COMPILED) and listed in the report's not_compiled, with its shape. That includes every use of a term n10s never compiles: sh:languageIn, sh:uniqueLang, sh:lessThan, sh:lessThanOrEquals, sh:equals, sh:qualifiedValueShape with sh:qualifiedMinCount, sh:qualifiedMaxCount and sh:qualifiedValueShapesDisjoint, sh:not, sh:and, sh:or, sh:xone, SHACL-SPARQL, sh:node on a property shape, and sh:targetNode, sh:targetSubjectsOf and sh:targetObjectsOf. It does not fail the run: the check step ran every shape on exactly the triples that were loaded (rules 1 and 2), and the round trip (rule 16) shows the graph holds exactly those triples. On a real multi-module ontology most such rows were shapes the engine does not apply to a class: shapes inside sh:or or sh:not, a node shape reached through a property shape's sh:node, untyped shapes.

    in_graph_shapes.py also prints a PREDICTION of the rows, made by running the selection patterns of n10s's PROP_CONSTRAINT_QUERY (lines 72 to 74 and 84 to 94) and NODE_CONSTRAINT_QUERY (lines 125 to 151) over the shapes with rdflib. It is a dry run for reading the shapes before a load and gates nothing; the report records where it and the engine differ (prediction_differences), and the engine is right.

    Why: a constraint the engine cannot run, or runs differently, reports silence or a false failure, and silence looks like a pass. Reading the engine's own list removes the need to reproduce its parser.

  1. Test every compiled row with one change that must fail, before you trust its silence, and re-run the tests on every new engine release. load_verify.py plans one case per listShapes() row (fail_cases). Each case runs in a transaction it rolls back, creates its own node with the row's target label and the uri urn:lpg-projection:fail-case:<n>, and gives it exactly what breaks that one row, so it needs no matching data. The case passes when n10s.validation.shacl.validate() reports that node (focusNode) with one of the row's expected components (EXPECTED in load_verify.py; the propertyShape column, a full IRI such as http://www.w3.org/ns/shacl#CountConstraintComponent) on the row's path (resultPath, the path's full IRI; for a closed shape, the property the case added). A node holding only what the case gave it breaks other rows too; matching the path and the component keeps those apart. Whether a path is a property or a relationship comes from the shapes (sh:datatype, a length or a range means a value; sh:class or sh:nodeKind sh:IRI means a node), else from the data and the ontology. The generated changes:
    RowChange on the new nodeExpected component
    sh:minCount n, n ≥ 1 (also on an inverse path)n − 1 values or relationships: the near miss, so a check enforcing a weaker minimum stays silentCountConstraintComponent or MinCountConstraintComponent
    sh:maxCount n on a valuen + 1 values of the declared datatype (dates as date(...))CountConstraintComponent or MaxCountConstraintComponent
    sh:maxCount n on a relationship (also inverse)n + 1 relationships to (or from) new nodesthe same
    sh:datatypea value of another type (0 for xsd:string, else a string)DatatypeConstraintComponent
    sh:class, sh:in of IRIsa relationship to a new node with no classClassConstraintComponent, InConstraintComponent
    sh:nodeKind sh:IRIa string property in place of the relationshipNodeKindConstraintComponent
    sh:nodeKind sh:Literala relationship in place of the valueNodeKindConstraintComponent
    sh:hasValue of an IRInone: the node lacks the valueHasValueConstraintComponent
    sh:disjoint (listed as sh:hasValue)the same value under both propertiesDisjointConstraintComponent
    ranges, sh:minLength, sh:maxLengtha value just outside the bound (sh:minLength n: a string of n − 1 characters)ValueRangeConstraintComponent, LengthConstraintComponent
    sh:closeda property the shape does not declare; and the compiled sh:ignoredProperties must equal the shape's list exactly, or the case fails without running (a wider compiled list would let n10s accept properties the file forbids)ClosedConstraintComponent
    node-level sh:classthe target label without the class's labelClassConstraintComponent

    n10s 2025.06.1 reports CountConstraintComponent, not the Min or Max component, whenever one property shape states both sh:minCount and sh:maxCount (SHACLValidator.java, lines 575 to 578), so the expected set keeps it; the near-miss counts are what keep a minimum's case from passing on a maximum's violation, and the reverse.

    A row nothing can break (sh:minCount 0, sh:minLength 0, a node-level sh:class naming the target itself) is a no-op. A row the generator cannot build a case for (for example sh:nodeKind sh:BlankNode, or a row on a sh:targetQuery shape) has status no case and fails the run, every run, until --manual-cases gives one: a JSON list of {"target", "path", "param", "cypher"}, where the Cypher changes one node and returns its uri as focus. A manual case runs like a generated one, with any path accepted. Nothing is carried from an earlier report: every run reruns every case. On the library template with extra shapes for each term (2026-10-23), 37 cases passed and 2 were no-ops; on a real multi-module ontology, 588 rows gave 507 passing cases and 77 no-ops.

    Why: the n10s behaviour behind the subset, and this table, came from such tests and from n10s's source, not from its documentation.

Verify (SKILL.md step 6)#

  1. Run SHACL in the graph and require zero violations; then prove the check can fail. Commit a deliberate mutant: remove one literal value a loaded sh:minCount shape requires, validate, require at least one violation on that node, restore the value, and require zero violations again. load_verify.py does it on the first compiled sh:minCount of at least 1 on a literal value that some node holds: it walks the candidates in order (mutant_targets) and fails the run only when no node holds any of them: 
    MATCH (n:`lib__Authorship`) WHERE n.`lib__position` IS NOT NULL WITH n ORDER BY n.uri LIMIT 1
RETURN n.uri AS uri, n.`lib__position` AS value;                       // keep both
MATCH (n:Resource {uri: $uri}) REMOVE n.`lib__position`;                 // the mutant
CALL n10s.validation.shacl.validate() YIELD focusNode RETURN focusNode;  // must list $uri
MATCH (n:Resource {uri: $uri}) SET n.`lib__position` = $value;          // restore

    Record the violation counts before and after the restore in the report. Why: zero violations from a check that cannot fire looks the same as a pass.

  1. Export the resources and diff against loadable.nt plus inferred.nt: zero triples lost, zero added. Export with: 
    CALL n10s.rdf.export.cypher('MATCH (n:Resource) OPTIONAL MATCH (n)-[r]->(m) RETURN n, r, m')
YIELD subject, predicate, object, isLiteral, literalType, literalLang
RETURN subject, predicate, object, isLiteral, literalType, literalLang

    Then:

    • drop every row whose subject, predicate or (IRI) object is in neo4j://graph.schema#: those are the n4sch__ schema nodes and properties onto.import added, not data;
    • build a tagged literal from object and literalLang when literalLang is set: with keepLangTag, n10s stores "Lending@en" but the export usually returns the text without the tag and sets literalLang to en;
    • when literalLang is empty and the type is xsd:string (or empty), split a trailing tag off the text with ^(.*)@([A-Za-z]{1,8}(?:-[A-Za-z0-9]{1,8})*)$ matched with DOTALL (Python re.S): n10s 2025.06.1 exports a tagged string that holds a newline as xsd:string "text@en" with no literalLang. The split is safe because rule 3 refused every source string that ends like a tag;
    • normalise both sides the same way, so the diff compares values, not spellings: a plain literal and an xsd:string literal with the same text are equal (RDF 1.1); integers load as INTEGER and export as xsd:long, so compare them as integers; decimals load as FLOAT and export as xsd:double, so compare them as doubles (rule 3 refused the decimals for which that hides a change);
    • compare with rdflib's to_isomorphic and graph_diff.

    With Rule 4b, first rebuild the EdgeRecords from relationships that have a uri. Why: the diff is what proves the graph holds exactly what passed the check.

  1. Load twice into an empty database, the second time with the lines of loadable.nt shuffled (a fixed seed), and compare graph hashes. load_verify.py overwrites the import folder's copy of loadable.nt with its lines shuffled by random.Random(12).shuffle, loads it, and puts the sorted file back afterwards; the committed file never changes. On Community edition, which has one user database, empty it between loads: 
    MATCH (n) DETACH DELETE n;      // the data, the schema nodes and n10s's _GraphConfig, _NsPrefDef and _n10sValidatorConfig nodes
SHOW CONSTRAINTS YIELD name;    // then DROP CONSTRAINT `<name>` for each one listed

    Check that MATCH (n) RETURN count(n) and SHOW CONSTRAINTS both return nothing, then rerun the whole load script (rule 8), which recreates the constraint, the configuration and the prefixes. For a large graph, delete in batches (CALL { ... } IN TRANSACTIONS). The hash (graph_hash in load_verify.py, whose docstring is the full specification) is SHA-256 over canonical JSON of every :Resource node as [uri, sorted labels, properties] and every relationship between two :Resource nodes as [source uri, type, target uri, relationship uri or "", relationship properties], nodes sorted by uri and relationships by their first four fields; list values keep their stored order (the load sorted them); a value JSON cannot hold, such as a date, is written as {"type": <its Python type>, "value": <its string form>}, so it never hashes like a string of the same text. Schema nodes from onto.import are :Resource nodes and count; n10s's configuration nodes have no Resource label and do not. The raw row count of the export in rule 16 can differ between the two loads while the hashes and the exported triple sets are equal; compare the hashes and the triples, not the row counts. Why: equal hashes show the result does not depend on load order.

Running the projection: where each step runs, pins, reports and scale#

From references/running.md

Serves the load step (rule 5, the container) and the running step. Read it before the first load, when setting up the projection in a repository or its CI, and before each rerun. The scripts named here are in this skill's scripts/.

Rules#

  1. Split the steps by what they need. CI runs only what needs no Java and no Docker (each line is uv run --no-project --with rdflib python3 <script> ..., with --with pyshacl for validate_data.py): 
    check_projection_rules.py --config <config> --shapes <shapes>... --releases <folder> <data>...
validate_data.py --config <config> --shapes <shapes>... <data>...
build.py loadable --output <temporary>/loadable.nt <data>...
build.py check-serialised --loadable <temporary>/loadable.nt --inferred inferred.nt
validate_data.py --config <config> --shapes <shapes>... <temporary>/loadable.nt inferred.nt
build.py manifest --config <config> --shapes <shapes>... --loadable <temporary>/loadable.nt \
  --inferred inferred.nt --output projection-manifest.json --verify <data>...
build.py check-report --manifest projection-manifest.json --report projection-report.json

    A workstation runs reason (ROBOT needs Java 11 or later), then load and verify with load_verify.py against a Neo4j container (rule 5). Why: CI images rarely run Java and Docker together, and the committed report (rule 3) carries the workstation's result into CI.

  1. Pin every tool by version, and every downloaded jar by its SHA-256, and check the checksums before each run. Record the versions in the configuration's versions, which the manifest copies. For the tested versions:
    JarDownload URLSHA-256
    n10s 2025.06.1https://github.com/neo4j-labs/neosemantics/releases/download/2025.06.1/neosemantics-2025.06.1.jar4c461087e08405c7cb472ecfefc043e9e8ed93628ed74988e4fda1f1bac54b3e
    ROBOT 1.9.10https://github.com/ontodev/robot/releases/download/v1.9.10/robot.jar16a73c074f3df359a7338a84b4e0788785fe06117f931bb9796e9619ea776105

    Check with shasum -a 256 <jar>. If a checksum differs, stop: the file is not the one these rules were tested with. Take the n10s jar that matches the Neo4j version (n10s 2025.06.1 is built for Neo4j 2025.06). APOC is not downloaded: with NEO4J_PLUGINS='["apoc"]' the image copies the APOC jar it bundles into /plugins as apoc.jar (for neo4j:2025.06.2, SHA-256 4df40cea7444ea193d08f8a679aa998c498196fe149c8c02badb998f1c9580fb, from apoc-2025.06.2-core.jar). So pin the image instead: record its digest (docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' neo4j:2025.06.2; on 2026-10-23 it was sha256:0347fe5b1126dd328cc68a54449c2cf83636e348e2da1547abf62b2dbfad67f2), and let load_verify.py --plugins-dir record every jar's SHA-256 in the report. Why: a different jar changes which constraints run in the graph and how values round-trip.

  1. Commit a manifest and a report that go stale on their own. build.py manifest writes the manifest: the SHA-256 of each data and shape file, the triple counts, the input fingerprint (pipeline.md, rule 5), the shapes fingerprint (the SHA-256 of every shape file's bytes, concatenated in the order given), the Rule 4 option and its reason, the release exceptions and the versions; with --verify it fails when the committed manifest differs. load_verify.py writes the report, in the shape of templates/projection-report.json. Its fields:
    FieldMeaning
    input_fingerprint, shapes_fingerprintAs in the manifest.
    left_out_before_importOne object per term the import-safe shapes leave out: {"shape": <IRI or blank-node id>, "constraint": <predicate IRI>, "reason": <text>} (pipeline.md, rule 13).
    compiled, not_compiled, prediction_differencesThe listShapes() rows as read from the engine; each constraint of the shapes file with no matching row (target, path, param and value); and where the in_graph_shapes.py prediction and the engine differ, for information (pipeline.md, rule 13).
    shapes_import_rows, in_graph_shape_constraintsThe rows the shapes import returned, and the listShapes() count (pipeline.md, rule 11).
    shacl_violations_in_graphViolations after the load; must be 0.
    fail_casesOne object per compiled row: its target, path, param and value, the Cypher (generated, or from --manual-cases), the focus, the expected path and components, the components reported on that path, and a status: passed, no-op, failed or no case (pipeline.md, rule 14).
    mutant, in_graph_mutant_violationsThe mutant's focus and property, its violations (must be above 0) and the violations after the restore (must be 0).
    export_rows, schema_rows_skipped, roundtrip_lost, roundtrip_addedThe raw export rows, the schema rows left out, and the triples lost and added; the last two must be 0.
    determinism_hash_sorted, determinism_hash_shuffledMust be equal (pipeline.md, rule 17).
    nodes, relationships, schema_relationshipsCounts after the sorted load: every :Resource node (schema nodes included), every relationship between two :Resource nodes, and how many of those are n4sch__ schema relationships from onto.import. To compare data between runs, use nodes and relationships minus schema_relationships (the data relationships); the schema part changes whenever a class or property is added.
    versions, plugin_jars_sha256The configuration's versions, and each jar's SHA-256 in the plugins folder.
    export_predicate_countsTriples per predicate in the export, schema rows left out; the triple-store add-on compares a store with it (add-ons.md).
    passedtrue: load_verify.py writes the report only when every check passed.
    samplesUp to ten lost or added triples, five violations and five failed cases.

    build.py check-report fails when the report's fingerprints differ from the manifest's, or when any check in it did not pass: it needs passed: true, at least one fail case, a non-empty compiled list (a missing or empty one fails), a fail case for every row in it and every case passed or no-op, a mutant that caught a violation and was restored, equal hashes and zero round-trip differences. The template, with its empty values, fails on purpose. A report is written only at the end of a run that passed: load_verify.py deletes the report and <report>.failed when it starts, before it reads any flag, writes a temporary file beside the report and renames it into place only after every check passed. A run that stops leaves no report: a failed check writes its details to <report>.failed (exit 1), a driver, network or file error writes nothing (exit 1), and bad input writes nothing (exit 2). Why: a projection result that outlives its inputs, or a run that did not finish, is a false pass, and a shape can change while the loaded triples do not.

  1. Commit inferred.nt, the manifest and the report together, after one full workstation run. Keep loadable.nt, merged.ttl and the downloads out of the repository; they are rebuilt from the Turtle files. Why: the three describe one run, and CI compares them with each other.
  1. Run Neo4j in a container bound to localhost, with the pinned plugins, and remove it once check-report has passed, or when you stop. Use the neo4j:2025.06.2 image (Community edition), mount a plugins folder holding the checked n10s jar at /plugins and the import folder at /import, let the image install APOC, allow both procedure namespaces, and bind Bolt to 127.0.0.1 on a non-default port, with a password made for this run.

    The default way to start it is the skill's compose file, docker/compose.yaml, which pins the image by digest, fetches the n10s jar into the plugins folder and checks its SHA-256 before Neo4j starts, binds Bolt to 127.0.0.1, and takes the password from NEO4J_PASSWORD (never written in the file). It needs the same run folder as below (LPG_RUN, holding plugins/ and import/). From the docker/ folder, with the run folder made as below:

    . "<run folder>/run.env"
LPG_RUN="$RUN" NEO4J_PASSWORD="$PASSWORD" LPG_BOLT_PORT="$PORT" \
  docker compose -p "$CONTAINER" --profile neo4j up -d   # add --profile fuseki --build for add-on J

    Wait for the start with docker compose -p "$CONTAINER" logs neo4j showing Started., run steps 1 to 3 below, then remove everything with docker compose -p "$CONTAINER" --profile neo4j --profile fuseki down -v, which removes the containers and their anonymous /data and /logs volumes, as docker rm -f -v does. Pass --compose-project "$CONTAINER" to load_verify.py (in place of --container), so the clean-up line it prints is that down -v line. The manual recipe that follows is the reference for what the compose file does.

    The plugins folder must be writable: the image changes its owner and writes apoc.jar into it, so a read-only mount (:ro) stops the container. Make new folders for each run, and copy the checked n10s jar into the plugins folder, so the image never writes into the folder that holds your downloads.

    Agent tools often start a fresh shell for every command, so keep the run's settings in a file, not in shell variables: a mode-600 run.env in a new run folder, read at the start of each later command and deleted with the folder after removal. Pick a container name and a free host port for this run; the examples use lpg-projection and 17687.

    RUN=$(mktemp -d); chmod 711 "$RUN"; echo "$RUN"          # note this path; every later command starts from it
mkdir -m 755 "$RUN/plugins" "$RUN/import"
cp <downloads>/neosemantics-2025.06.1.jar "$RUN/plugins/"
( umask 077; printf 'CONTAINER=%q\nPORT=%q\nPASSWORD=%q\nRUN=%q\n' lpg-projection 17687 "$(openssl rand -hex 12)" "$RUN" > "$RUN/run.env" )
. "$RUN/run.env"
docker run -d --name "$CONTAINER" -p "127.0.0.1:$PORT:7687" \
  -e NEO4J_AUTH="neo4j/$PASSWORD" -e NEO4J_PLUGINS='["apoc"]' \
  -e NEO4J_dbms_security_procedures_unrestricted='apoc.*,n10s.*' \
  -v "$RUN/import":/import -v "$RUN/plugins":/plugins \
  neo4j:2025.06.2@sha256:0347fe5b1126dd328cc68a54449c2cf83636e348e2da1547abf62b2dbfad67f2

    The chmod 711 on the run folder and 755 on the two mounted folders matter: a folder only its owner can open (what mktemp -d makes) stops the container at once ("Folder /plugins is not accessible for user: neo4j"), while run.env itself stays readable by you alone.

    Then wait for the start, and stop on a failure. The check is a function that returns, so a failure ends the command and not your shell:

    . "<run folder>/run.env"
wait_for_neo4j() {
  for i in $(seq 1 60); do
    docker logs "$CONTAINER" 2>&1 | grep -q 'Started.' && return 0
    [ "$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Running}}' "$CONTAINER")" = true ] || { docker logs "$CONTAINER" 2>&1 | tail -20; return 1; }
    docker logs "$CONTAINER" 2>&1 | grep -q ' ERROR ' && { docker logs "$CONTAINER" 2>&1 | tail -20; return 1; }
    sleep 3
  done
  echo 'Neo4j did not start in 180 seconds'; return 1
}
wait_for_neo4j

    Then, in this order, each command starting with . "<run folder>/run.env":

    1. run load_verify.py as its docstring shows, with NEO4J_PASSWORD="$PASSWORD", --bolt "bolt://127.0.0.1:$PORT", --import-dir "$RUN/import", --plugins-dir "$RUN/plugins", --container "$CONTAINER" (or --compose-project "$CONTAINER" when you started it with the compose file) and the configuration, shape, data, merged.ttl, loadable.nt, inferred.nt and --report arguments. It prints its next step with that container name;
    2. if it exits 1 or 2, stop here and do not run check-report. No report exists then; on exit 1 after the database checks, <report>.failed holds the values. The run deleted the report path when it started, so if that path is the committed report, restore it (git restore projection-report.json) and never stage <report>.failed. To try again after a fix (a case with status no case needs a manual case in a --manual-cases file, pipeline.md, rule 14), rerun step 1 while the container is still up; load_verify.py empties the database itself. If you stop instead, go to step 4. Every rerun runs every case again;
    3. run build.py check-report --manifest projection-manifest.json --report projection-report.json, as in rule 1; if you copy the graph to another Neo4j, such as Aura (add-ons.md, add-on I), do it now, while the container is up;
    4. only then docker rm -f -v "$CONTAINER" (with the compose file, docker compose -p "$CONTAINER" --profile neo4j --profile fuseki down -v), then delete the run folder with its run.env. If you stop before check-report passes, do the same anyway; docker ps -a then lists no projection container. The -v removes the container's anonymous /data and /logs volumes; without it each run leaves them behind, and after a few runs Docker's disk fills and Neo4j fails to start ("Database name 'system' is invalid"). Why: the load script reads file:///import/...; Community edition has one user database, so the determinism check empties it between loads (pipeline.md, rule 17); and a forgotten container with a known password is an open database on the workstation.
  1. Change only the loader as the graph grows:
    SizeLoaderWhat changes
    Up to about 10M triplesn10s rdf.import.fetchNothing
    About 10M to 1B+ triplesGenerate node and relationship CSVs from loadable.nt and inferred.nt with the same mapping, then neo4j-admin database importOnly the load step
    Incremental updatesLoad each delta with n10s (MERGE by uri); delete with n10s.rdf.deleteAdd a periodic full rebuild and compare hashes

    Why: the mapping rules do not depend on size, so the checks and the verify step stay valid.

  1. Explore a graph read-only through the official Neo4j MCP server. Neo4j's MCP server (https://github.com/neo4j/mcp, README at commit 1210b0e8f0, read 2026-10-24) gives an agent get-schema, read-cypher, write-cypher and list-gds-procedures on a running Neo4j. Point it at the verified local graph or its Aura copy with NEO4J_MCP_READ_ONLY=true, which disables write-cypher. That is a guard, not a boundary: the README warns that read-cypher relies on Neo4j classifying each query as read-only, and "custom procedures or functions incorrectly classified as read-only by Neo4j may bypass this check". For a hard boundary, give the server a database user with read-only privileges (on Aura, a read-only role), and do not install custom procedures you have not reviewed. Why: the graph is a projection of the Turtle release; a fix made through the server would be lost at the next rebuild and would break the hash that proves the copy (add-ons.md, add-on I).

One run, every store, every check: run_projection.py#

From references/run-config.md

Read it when a project projects its release more than once, or into more than one store, and wants one command instead of its own scripts around this skill's. run_projection.py runs steps 2 to 6, add-ons F, H, I, J and K, the rdf-store skill's round trips and a rebuild from any store, all from one run configuration, and runs every check each of them has. It runs the skill's own scripts; it adds no check of its own except the rebuild's two comparisons.

uv run --no-project --with rdflib python3 scripts/run_projection.py --config run.json --plan
uv run --no-project --with rdflib python3 scripts/run_projection.py --config run.json [--only a,b] [--skip a,b]

--plan lists the steps that would run, and why any is skipped, and runs nothing. It needs uv, Docker, and Java 11 or later for ROBOT. It never prints a password: the local Neo4j's password is generated and kept in <out>/neo4j-run/run.env (mode 600). The target and Databricks env files are passed to the scripts by path, never read by the driver.

First, choose releases or files#

The run configuration's mode says what is projected. Without one, the driver prints this choice and stops, so ask the user before writing the configuration:

ModeWhat it takesForAgainst
releases (recommended)Versioned packages: each data file has one owl:versionIRI and pins what it requiresThe pins and the closure of requirements are checked, every node is tagged with its release, the module graph shows what requires what, and a store copy traces back to a releaseYou need packages first
filesAny Turtle or N-Triples files, or folders of themWorks on what you have now, with the same loads, hashes, round trips and rebuildNo version pins or closure check; without SHACL shapes the projection uses defaults derived from the data

When the user picks releases and has none, the driver stops and points to the ontology skill's guided packaging walk-through (skills/data/ontology/scripts/build_package.py), which builds them. The walk-through is being built separately; until it lands, package with the ontology skill's Step 10 (release and publication), or choose files.

The run configuration#

A JSON object. Paths are relative to the configuration's own folder, so it can sit in the project repository, beside the projection configuration. Copy templates/run-config.json.

KeyNeeded byWhat it holds
projection_configevery stepThe projection configuration (templates/projection-config.json).
modeevery stepreleases or files (above).
data, shapesevery stepReleases: the released package files, and the shape files (each release's and any whole-graph ones). Or give inputs_script instead. Files: shapes is optional.
filesfiles modeRDF files (.ttl, .nt) or folders; a folder gives every such file under it, in path order.
graphsfiles mode, optional{file: graph IRI} for a file with no owl:versionIRI.
inputs_scriptinstead of data and shapesA Python script printing one absolute path per line for <script> data and <script> shapes, when the project keeps its list elsewhere. It runs with rdflib, pySHACL and the neo4j driver.
releasesreleases modeThe folder of released packages, <module>/<X.Y.Z>/, for the pin check.
outevery stepThe output folder. It must be outside the repository that holds the configuration.
robot_jarprojectROBOT 1.9.10. Its SHA-256 is checked before any command runs (running.md, rule 2).
manual_casesload, optionalPassed to load_verify.py --manual-cases.
release_graphsjena, databricks, rebuildThe other files of each release that the store copy holds, by name without .ttl (for example ["shapes", "catalog"]): <name>.ttl beside each data file, loaded as the graph <version IRI>/<name>.
target_envcopyAn env file naming another Neo4j, such as Aura: NEO4J_URI, NEO4J_USERNAME, NEO4J_PASSWORD, optional NEO4J_DATABASE.
replace_targetcopy, optionaltrue passes --replace to copy_graph.py, which deletes everything on the target first. A rebuild that copies needs it, because the target then holds the first copy.
databricksdatabricks, a rebuild from Databricks{"env": <file>, "table": <catalog.schema.table>}; the env file is the one the rdf-store skill reads.
queriesexploreThe project's saved walks for explore.py compare.
rebuildrebuild{"source": "repo" or "jena" or "databricks", "out": <folder>}.
rdf_storejena, databricks, explore, rebuildThe rdf-store skill folder; by default ../rdf-store beside this skill.
neo4j, jena, explore_fuseki, triplestore_fusekioptional{"compose_project", "bolt_port"} or {"compose_project", "port"} for each container. The defaults are lpg-local on Bolt 17711, lpg-jena on 13031, lpg-explore on 13032 and lpg-triplestore on 13030.
keep_neo4joptionaltrue leaves the local Neo4j running at the end; otherwise it is removed.
separatorload, review, tags, optionalWhat sits between a prefix and a local name in the kept graph: "_" for one underscore. n10s writes two; with another value every check runs on n10s's names first, then every label, relationship type and property key is renamed, the rename is proven lossless (rename_lossless in the report), and the hashes are of the renamed graph.

A step whose key is missing is skipped and says so: no target_env, no copy; no databricks, no Databricks round trip. A step that needs an earlier one's output or the local Neo4j stops with a message when it isn't there. Run load in the same run as the steps that read the local graph.

Files mode#

Each file is one named graph. Its name is its owl:versionIRI when it has one; else its entry in graphs; else urn:ontology-to-lpg:file: and its path relative to the run configuration. A graphs entry for a file that has an owl:versionIRI is refused, so the store and Neo4j always name a file alike. Every store gets each file under that name (rdfstore.py --graph FILE=IRI), module_tags.py --graph tags each node and relationship with it, and explore.py --files reads every graph in the store as a package.

Without shapes, the driver writes default-shapes.ttl into out: one sh:NodeShape per class the data types a node with (outside the RDF, RDFS, OWL, SHACL and XSD namespaces), and for each predicate the class's instances use (subclasses' instances included), a property shape with the counts the data shows: sh:maxCount the most values one instance has, and sh:minCount 1 when every instance has one. The inverse ends of the qualified-relation classes the projection configuration registers get a shape on sh:inversePath, counted the same way, as Rule 4a requires. The data conforms by construction, and the load's gates (compiled rows, a fail case each, the mutant) have something to check. n10s's defaults decide the rest: a literal becomes a property, an IRI a relationship.

The rule check runs without --releases, so version pins and the closure of requirements are not checked. The run says so, and so does run-manifest.json.

The run manifest#

The project step writes <out>/run-manifest.json: the mode, each data and shape file with its SHA-256 (and, in files mode, its graph name and where the name came from), whether the shapes were derived, and the notes above. The rebuild refuses to compare with out when any of those files has changed since.

The steps and their checks#

StepWhat runsIt passes when
projectcheck_projection_rules.py, validate_data.py, build.py merge, ROBOT ELK, build.py inferred, loadable, check-serialised, validate_data.py again on both files, build.py manifest, then the advisory in_graph_shapes.pyevery script exits 0: checks V1 to V5 (multi-store.md)
loadNeo4j with n10s from docker/compose.yaml, load_verify.py --compose-project, build.py check-reportthe report is written and check-report passes: V6 to V12. A failure removes the container.
reviewmodel_review.py on the local graph, written to model-review.jsonno ERROR finding
tagsmodule_tags.py tag, check, modules on the local graph (add-on F)every node and relationship carries exactly one tag, equal to its package
graph-typebuild.py graph-type to graph-type.cypher (add-on H)the statement is written; apply it by hand
triplestoreFuseki from docker/compose.yaml, triplestore.py (add-on J)the per-graph, per-predicate and three-way counts match the report
copycopy_graph.py to target_env (add-on I), then module_tags.py check and modules and model_review.py therethe target's graph hash equals the source's and the report's, the tags check passes there, and no ERROR finding
jenathe rdf-store skill's Fuseki and rdfstore.py roundtrip of the data files and their release graphs (files mode: each file under its graph name)the store's export has the files' RDFC-1.0 hash
databricksrdfstore.py roundtrip --store databricks of the same dataset (add-on K)the same, for the Delta table; the table is replaced only by a staging copy with that hash
explorea second Fuseki holding the data and inferred.nt, then explore.py compare against the local graph and, when this run copied, against the targetevery saved walk and the module map give the same edges, nodes and tags in Neo4j and in Jena
rebuildsee belowthe store's export hashes equal to the release, the rebuild's triples and graph hashes equal this run's, and its own load, tags, copy and walks pass

The rebuild#

rebuild proves the graph can be rebuilt from a store's copy alone. It needs project and load to have run into out (in this run or an earlier one), with the inputs run-manifest.json records, and removes this run's local Neo4j first, because the rebuild loads its own on the same port.

  1. With source jena or databricks, it exports everything the store holds (rdfstore.py export --ttl-dir), packs the release files the same way the round trip did, and requires equal RDFC-1.0 hashes (rdfstore.py compare). A rebuild from Jena loads Jena first when this run hasn't. With repo, it takes the repository files.
  2. It maps the exported graphs to the inputs. A data file maps to the graph named by its owl:versionIRI (in files mode, by its graph name), and a release graph's shapes file to <version IRI>/<name>. A shape file that is no release graph, such as a whole-graph shapes file, was never in the store, so it comes from the repository, and the run says which.
  3. It runs project and load into rebuild.out, then requires loadable.nt and inferred.nt to hold the first run's triples, compared as RDF 1.1 terms, and both reports to hold exactly determinism_hash_sorted and determinism_hash_shuffled, non-empty and equal to the first run's. A store export may write a literal typed xsd:string as a plain literal, which RDF 1.1 defines as the same term, so the files need not be byte-equal. The equal graph hashes prove Neo4j holds the same graph.
  4. It tags, copies when target_env is set (with replace_target), and explores when queries is set.

run_projection.py compare-triples <rebuild out> <baseline out> and compare-reports <rebuild report> <baseline report> run step 3's two checks on their own.

What it leaves behind#

Every Fuseki is removed when the run ends, pass or fail, and the local Neo4j too unless keep_neo4j is set. Each removal runs even when another fails. A removal that fails fails the run, even when every step passed, and the run says which; a step's own failure is still the one reported. A copy stays on the target, and a Databricks round trip leaves the table holding the release. To empty them, delete only what the run loaded.

Add-ons and anti-patterns#

From references/add-ons.md

Read it when a consumer asks for something the core pipeline does not give (superclass labels, split language keys, exact decimals, units, provenance, business keys, a GRAPH TYPE, the graph in Aura, the same data in a triple store or in Databricks), or when reviewing a projection.

Add-ons (adopt only when needed, and record each)#

Add-onUse whenWhat to add
